newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Yield curves guide to recessions - BIS economists.
newsitem.headline: Yield curves guide to recessions - BIS economists.

text.p: Yield curves can be used for predicting recessions in major countries and are a good candidate as monetary policy indicators for central banks, according to a working paper by two economists at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
The term structure of interest rates contained useful information for predicting recessions as much as six to eight quarters ahead in eight major economies, the paper said.

This contrasts with standard leading indicators, which are only useful for predicting recessions in the immediate future, such as one to three quarters ahead, BIS economists Stefan Gerlach and Henri Bernard said.
The power of term spreads to predict recessions between 1972 and 1993 was strongest in Germany, Canada and the United States, while it was lower for Japan, the paper said.
One plausible reason was the difference in financial market regulation and that interest rates in Japan did not accurately reflect financial market's expectations, the paper said.
The eight countries examined by Gerlach and Bernard were the United States, Germany, Japan, Canada, United Kingdom, France, the Netherlands and Belgium.
Many central banks already include term structures as one of the many indicators they examine for signs of future economic trends and as a guide to monetary policy.
One reason is that economists in the early 1990s showed that spreads between long and short term interest rates, or term spreads, contained information about future U.S. inflation.
More recently economists also found that the term structure of interest rates also was a useful indicator of recession, especially in the U.S.
The aim of Gerlach and Bernard was to see whether this also was true for a wider number of countries.
"While the results vary between countries, in all countries spreads do contain information about the probability of recessions in the future," the report said, adding:
"The predictive ability is found to be highest in Germany, followed by the United States and Canada, and lowest in Japan."

Among the reasons that term spreads are particularly attractive as monetary policy indicators is that they are instantanously available, they are never revised, and are available for for much longer time horizons that standard forecasts, which are typically limited to one or two years.

The paper, called "Does the term structure predict recessions ? The International Evidence", used recession data similar to those by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), an influential U.S. non-governmental think tank.
